tip: Separable verbs split: 'aankomen' sends its prefix 'aan' to the end of the clause: 'kwamen wij te laat aan'.
In an 'als' clause the verb goes last ('is'), but the main clause keeps the verb second: 'als het mooi weer is, gaan wij' (if the weather is nice, go we).
Here 'als' means 'as' in the sense of a role, not if or when: 'werkt zij als arts' = works as a doctor.
A command is just the verb stem: 'zet' from 'zetten' (to put, set). Add 'u' for formal ('zet u') or 'laten we' for 'let's'.
A helper verb like 'kon' (could) sends the main verb to the end in its base form: 'dat je kon komen'.
Dutch commands normally use the bare verb stem with no subject: 'rijd' is just the stem of 'rijden' (drive).
'Schoonmaken' is a separable verb, so in a command the 'schoon' splits off to the end: 'maak de keuken schoon'.
'Wees' is the special command form of 'zijn' (to be); there is no 'ben' used as a command.
In a passive, 'door' marks who does the action, the 'by': 'de les wordt door de leraar gegeven'.
Completed passives use 'is' plus the participle and drop 'geworden': 'de wedstrijd is door het thuisteam gewonnen'.
After a short vowel plus l, m, n or r, the diminutive doubles that consonant and adds '-etje': 'pil' becomes 'pilletje'.
'Het spijt me' is the set phrase for 'I'm sorry', literally 'it grieves me', with 'me' as the person affected.
'In plaats van' is the fixed phrase for 'instead of', here followed by a noun: 'in plaats van de lift'.
'Genieten' pairs with 'van' to mean 'enjoy': 'geniet van de maaltijd', never 'geniet de maaltijd'.
'Denken' takes 'aan' to mean think of or remember: 'denk aan je afspraak', not 'denk je afspraak'.
The '-je' ending adds smallness or warmth, so 'berichtje' is a short, friendly note, softer than 'bericht'.
'Omdat' and 'want' both mean because, but 'omdat' sends the verb to the clause end while 'want' keeps normal order: 'omdat het hard regent' (because it is raining hard).
When a clause comes first, the verb comes before the subject: 'wanneer het donker wordt, doen wij'.
'Nadat' (after) sends its clause's verb to the end: 'nadat de storm voorbij was'.
'Worden' marks the ongoing or future action ('zal worden bezorgd', will be delivered) while 'zijn' marks the finished state ('is verstuurd', has been sent).
In an 'om ... te' clause, 'te' goes directly before the infinitive at the end: 'om de deur op slot te doen'.
'Hoewel' already means 'although' and carries the contrast, so you do not add 'maar': 'hoewel hij erg moe was'.
Diminutives are always het-words: 'de tuin' becomes 'het tuintje' even though 'tuin' itself is a de-word.
'Heb' is the command form of 'hebben', and 'heb geduld' is the set way to say be patient (literally have patience).
'Een beetje' means 'a little' with uncountable things: 'ik spreek een beetje Nederlands'.
Diminutives make their plural with '-s': 'broodje' becomes 'broodjes' and 'gebakje' becomes 'gebakjes'.
'Aankleden' is reflexive here: the 'je' in 'kleed je netjes aan' refers back to yourself.
Movement verbs like 'aankomen' take 'zijn' in the perfect, not 'hebben': 'je bent veilig aangekomen'.
'Dag' works as both hello and goodbye in Dutch, so 'dag' here means bye.
Language names stay capitalized in Dutch, even mid-sentence: 'Nederlands'.
